rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to 13:15 and 16:48–49 for the meaning of prostration in this verse.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of this "prostration", see 13:15 and 16:48~9, and the corresponding notes.

words: مَن فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَن فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders the relative pronoun man as including all things and beings, following his explanation at 13:15.
rows.anchor: My rendering of the relative pronoun man, in this context, as "all [things and beings] that..." is explained in note 33 on 13:15.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Razi
rows.claim: Zamakhshari and Razi parse the interpolated phrase as an elliptically implied predicate linked to the preceding nominal subject.
rows.anchor: According to Zamakhshari and Razi, this interpolated phrase - with its stress on "consciously" - is an elliptically implied predicate (khabar) linked with the preceding nominal subject (mubtada'):

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All creation prostrates willingly or unwillingly, but many humans do not submit consciously; compare 13:15.
rows.anchor: although everything in creation "prostrates itself" before God, willingly or unwillingly (cf. 13:15), not all human beings do so consciously.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suffering due to many is the necessary consequence of their worldly attitude, not an arbitrary punishment in the conventional sense.
rows.anchor: as a necessary consequence and corollary of his attitude in this world, and not as an arbitrary "punishment" in the conventional sense of this term.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses God's repelling some people by means of others and links the phrase to 2:251.
rows.anchor: Lit., "were it not that God repels some people by means of others" (cf. the identical phrase in the second paragraph of 2:251).

words: وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلنَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defending religious freedom is the foremost cause for which arms may and must be taken up; without it corruption would overwhelm the earth.
rows.anchor: The implication is that the defence of religious freedom is the foremost cause for which arms may and, indeed, must - be taken up

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mansak means a way of worship and can also denote an act of worship.
rows.anchor: Lit., "a way of worship" (mansak, which sometimes denotes also "an act of worship").

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the fuller explanation, Asad points to the second paragraph of 5:48 and its notes 66–68.
rows.anchor: For a fuller emplanation of this passage, see the second paragraph of 5:48 - "Unto every one of you have We appointed a [different] law and way of life" - and the corresponding notes 66-68.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Baghawi
rows.claim: Zamakhshari and Baghawi understand the instruction as not allowing oneself to be drawn into disputes.
rows.anchor: I.e., do not allow thyself to be drawn into disputes" (Zamakhshari and Baghawi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The new creation is a distinct creature existing independently of the mother's body.
rows.anchor: Lit., "as another creature", i.e., existing independently of the mother's body.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabari notes that Arabs call artisans creators; since God alone is Creator in the primary sense, ahsan al-khaliqin uses khaliq secondarily.
rows.anchor: As Tabari points out, the Arabs apply the designation "creator" to every artisan (sani')

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The categorical ban connects with the preceding passages by adding protection against possible slander.
rows.anchor: This categorical prohibition connects with the preceding passages inasmuch as it serves as an additional protection of individuals against possible slander.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rule establishes each person's home and private life as inviolable, with wider socio-political implications.
rows.anchor: In its wider purport, it postulates the inviolability of each person's home and private life.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Razi
rows.claim: Zamakhshari and Razi take the rhetorical question as a factual assertion that Pharaoh's people refuse to become conscious of God.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari and Razi understand this rhetorical question in the sense apparent in my rendering, namely, as a statement of fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated construction expresses utter condemnation of Moses' deed; Asad's inserted "heinous" makes that force explicit.
rows.anchor: a construction meant to express the speaker's utter condemnation of the deed referred to: hence, my interpolation of the word "heinous".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal threat says Noah will surely be among those stoned to death.
rows.anchor: Lit., "thou wilt surely be among those who are stoned [to death)".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to the account of Hud and ʿAd at 7:65 and its note 48.
rows.anchor: See 7:65 and the corresponding note 48.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to the account of Salih and Thamud at 7:73 and to the version at 2:61–68.
rows.anchor: For the story of Salih and the tribe of Thamud, see 7:73 and the corresponding note 56; also, the version appearing in ii: 61-68.

rows.speaker: Mujahid
rows.claim: Mujahid, as quoted by Tabari, interprets God's seeing Muhammad when he stands as wherever he may be.
rows.anchor: According to Mujahid (as quoted by Tabari), this means "wherever thou mayest be".

rows.speaker: Other commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators limit the phrase to standing for prayer; Asad rejects this as too narrow compared with Mujahid's broader reading.
rows.anchor: Other commentators take it to mean "when thou standest up for prayer", but this seems to be too narrow an interpretation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees Muhammad among the believers, in contrast to those who disobey him in 26:216.
rows.anchor: I.e., among the believers. as contrasted with those who "disobey thee" (see verse 216 above).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affak literally means a great or habitual liar; here it means one who lies to himself, a self-deceiver who readily lies to others too.
rows.anchor: The term affak which literally denotes "a great [or "habitual"] liar", has here the meaning of "one who lies to himself":

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari explains hawlaha as meaning "around it."
rows.anchor: Thus Zamakhshari explains the expression hawlaha (lit., "around it").

words: بُورِكَ مَن فِى ٱلنَّارِ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا
rows.speaker: some of the earliest commentators, quoted by Tabari
rows.claim: Early commentators read the fire as the light God bestows on prophets; Asad supposes their spiritual sensitivity makes them inherently near it.
rows.anchor: According to some of the earliest commentators, quoted by Tabari, the "fire" (nar) is in this context synonymous with "light" (nur),

words: بُورِكَ مَن فِى ٱلنَّارِ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may refer to God's own light, which encompasses and is the core of all spiritual illumination.
rows.anchor: Alternatively, the phrase man fi 'n-nar wa-man hawlaha may be 'inderstood as referring to God's Own light, which encompasses, and is the core of, all spiritual illumination.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to 20:17–20 for comparison with this account of Moses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to note 14 on 20:20–21 for a tentative explanation of the symbolism of the staff miracle.
rows.anchor: For a tentative explanation of the symbolism underlying the miracle of the staff, see note 14 on 20:2O~2l.

words: لَا تَخَفْ إِنِّى لَا يَخَافُ لَدَىَّ ٱلْمُرْسَلُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders illa here as "and neither" and points to his explanation at 4:29.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of illa, in this context, as "and neither", see note 38 on 4:29.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What God gave Solomon includes worldly wealth as well as faith, wisdom, and insight into normally hidden realities.
rows.anchor: I.e., not only worldly wealth but also faith, wisdom and an insight into realities normally hidden from other men.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon characterizes them as people who prize material things alone and lack awareness of spiritual values.
rows.anchor: I.e., people who prize only material things and have no inkling of spiritual values.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Pharaoh's household that found Moses was Pharaoh's own wife, as the next verse and 66:11 indicate.
rows.anchor: As is evident from the next verse as well as from 66: 1], it was Pharaoh's own wife.
